extraction.document_type: Journal article (original article) with pre-registered analyses
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 761 lines of the _text file (about 61.6k chars), including references and the cite block. Paul's markup: none. No file in _annots/ (63 JSON files) references hash 67b4400dd0c4 or the title, and no file in annotations/ mentions Ornstein or the title, so paul_markup is empty. Metadata corrections: the hint DOI (from PII S2049847024000645) does not match the DOI printed in the text, which is 10.1017/psrm.2024.64; the journal is Political Science Research and Methods, not a Cambridge book; the year is 2025 by volume (accepted 2024). Topic coverage: lobbying, network analysis, path-finding, allocation, and persuasion/turnout are absent. Legislators appear only through House floor speeches (virtue-praise labels by party). Elections appear only through campaign-ad tone; no vote, turnout, or persuasion outcome is modeled.
extraction.research_question: Can few-shot prompts to large language models (GPT-3, GPT-4) be adapted, without task-specific training or large labeled sets, to political text-as-data tasks (sentiment classification, ad tone classification, ideology scaling, topic discovery), matching or beating conventional automated methods and approaching expert or crowd coding at far lower cost? The paper also asks what validation and prompt-design practices make such measures trustworthy.
extraction.theory: Text-as-data measurement (Grimmer and Stewart 2013: "validation, validation, validation"). Contextualized word embeddings and transformer self-attention let word meaning depend on context (Vaswani et al. 2017), so context-dependent labels such as sarcasm can be learned from a prompt rather than from a trained classifier. Few-shot in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020). For topics, the expectation that conservatives praise loyalty, patriotism and hard work while liberals praise fairness, compassion and charity follows Moral Foundations Theory (Graham et al. 2009), p.275.
extraction.data: Four applications. (1) 945 tweets referencing the US Supreme Court within 24 hours of Masterpiece Cakeshop (2018) and of Trump v. Mazars and Trump v. Vance (2020); unit = tweet; author-coded 7-point sentiment from -1 to +1 after two-stage manual coding (1000 labeled, 55 dropped, 945 kept; Fleiss kappa 0.72). Benchmark classifier trained on 1.2 million tweets from Go et al. (2009). (2) 935 political ads from Carlson and Montgomery (2017); unit = ad; expert ratings and crowd pairwise comparisons (9420 tasks at 6 cents, $565.20 total). (3) 18,263 sentences from 18 British party manifestos, 1987-2010; crowd-coded per Benoit et al. (2016), with an expert-score benchmark. (4) 9,704 one-minute US House floor speeches in the 113th Congress (2013-2014) from Wilkerson and Casas (2017); 9,565 analyzed because 139 speeches over 6,000 characters were omitted for API token limits (fn. 8, p.275). Models: GPT-3 (175B parameters) and GPT-4; GPT-3 was removed from the public API in January 2024 (p.278).
extraction.method: Few-shot prompting. The LLM returns a next-word probability vector over labels, and continuous measures are built from it. Sentiment (tweets): six few-shot examples, two per class (positive, neutral, negative), with a preamble describing the ruling; the continuous measure is the first principal component of the probability vector (pre-registered via AsPredicted 92341, 92422, 92666, 100718, 125217; p.267-268). Ad tone: one-shot prompt (Figure 3), continuous tone from the probability vector. Ideology: one-shot Policy Prompt applied per sentence; sentence score = P(Conservative) minus P(Liberal); averaged to economic and social passage means per manifesto (p.273). GPT-4 ideology deviated from the pre-registered protocol and used the Le Mens and Gallego (2023) whole-document prompt (p.273). Topics: prompt asks GPT-3 for virtue labels; 51,483 labels returned, about 5-6 per speech, grouped by synonyms (p.275-276). Benchmarks: dictionary sentiment, Naive Bayes (bag of words), TweetNLP (RoBERTa fine-tuned on tweets, Camacho-Collados et al. 2022). Appendix A has zero-shot and one-shot variants (not in the text file).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is measurement validation: each LLM measure is correlated with or compared against human gold labels (author codes, expert ratings, crowd codes), and topic labels are validated by an optimal-label task in which a blinded coder picks the best of four labels for 400 speeches (80 percent agreed with GPT-3's label, chance 25 percent; p.276).
extraction.scope: Population and era: US tweets about SCOTUS decisions (2018-2020); US campaign ads from the Carlson and Montgomery (2017) corpus (dates not stated in text); UK party manifestos 1987-2010; US House one-minute floor speeches 2013-2014. Models: GPT-3 and GPT-4 (2023-2024 API). The paper argues about political science text-as-data generally, and cautions about closed proprietary models and about tasks needing current or factual information (p.278-279).

key_findings.finding: Sentiment on 945 SCOTUS tweets: GPT-3 few-shot correctly predicts negative/positive in 88.4 percent of cases; TweetNLP 64.3 percent; best dictionary method 38.3 percent; Naive Bayes trained on 1.2M tweets 57.7 percent.

GPT-4 performs slightly worse than GPT-3 on the sentiment task; its probabilities are poorly calibrated and overconfident; for over 70 percent of posts GPT-4 gives a single-label probability above 99 percent; it returns Neutral more often than the authors.
key_findings.numbers: over 70% of posts with >99% probability

key_findings.finding: Ad tone: LLM coding of 935 ads took under one minute and cost $0.60, against $565.20 for crowd pairwise coding (9420 tasks at 6 cents), about a 1000-fold cost reduction. The LLM tone measure is said to correlate with expert ratings as strongly as the crowd measure; the text gives no coefficient for this.
key_findings.location: Section 3.2, p.269 (crowd cost lines 326-327) and p.271 (lines 355-358)
key_findings.numbers: $0.60 vs $565.20; 935 ads; under 1 minute

key_findings.finding: Ideology scaling of 18 UK manifestos: LLM scores correlate with expert ratings at rho = 0.92 on the economic dimension and rho = 0.8 on the social dimension; better at between-party than within-party variance (true for crowd codes too).
key_findings.numbers: rho 0.92 economic; rho 0.8 social

key_findings.finding: Cost of ideology scoring: about $2.50 for 18,263 sentences with GPT-3, against about $3,226.70 for the original crowd coding (footnote assumes 1.5 cents per sentence and 215,107 crowd evaluations).
key_findings.numbers: $2.50 vs ~$3226.70; 18,263 sentences; 215,107 evaluations

key_findings.finding: Topic labeling of 9,565 House speeches returned 51,483 labels (about 5-6 per speech). Democrats more often praised advocacy (+3.5 pp), charity (+1.5), compassion (+3.9), education (+3.3), fairness (+3). Republicans more often praised bravery (+2), patriotism (+4.2), loyalty (+2.1), sacrifice (+2.8), success (+7.7).
key_findings.numbers: 51,483 labels; differences in percentage points as listed

key_findings.finding: Topic label validation: for 400 random speeches a blinded coder picked GPT-3's label over three random intruders in 80 percent of cases, against 25 percent chance.
key_findings.numbers: 80% vs 25% chance; n = 400

key_findings.finding: The model is not a dictionary method: 5,332 speeches contain the word honor, but GPT-3 labels only 145 as praising honor, nearly all about soldiers or veterans.
key_findings.numbers: 5,332 contain honor; 145 labeled as praising honor

key_findings.finding: Cost trend: computing cost of the paper's applications fell 97 percent between fall 2021 and publication.
key_findings.numbers: 97% decline

key_findings.finding: Reproducibility: GPT-3 models used were removed from the public API in January 2024, so exact results cannot be reproduced unless the weights are released.
key_findings.numbers: January 2024

key_findings.finding: Bias: GPT-3 answered 58 percent of 817 misconception questions truthfully (Lin et al. 2021), cited as a reason for caution on factual-accuracy tasks.

limitations: Results depend on researcher choices, especially prompt design; the authors recommend a three-step validation: hand-label a small set for prompt design, validate on a second hand-labeled set, then apply to the rest (p.277, lines 567-575).
GPT-4 is worse-calibrated than GPT-3 for next-word classification because of RLHF (p.268, lines 293-296; p.278, lines 587-597).
Reproducibility depends on proprietary, closed models that vendors may stop serving; the GPT-3 models used were retired from the API (p.278).
LLMs inherit human biases and falsehoods, including stereotyped embeddings, and can generate hate speech; RLHF mitigates this at some cost to accuracy (p.278, lines 611-624).
Authors advise against tasks that need up-to-date factual information (p.278-279).
Ad tone: model diverges from experts on attacks against unnamed targets, and on ads needing outside context; the authors argue one expert label is arguably miscoded (p.271, lines 359-368).
Sentiment: tweets whose meaning depends on outside political context can be misread unless the prompt supplies that context.
Pre-registration deviation: GPT-4 ideology used a different, non-pre-registered protocol (p.273, lines 433-440).
Speeches over 6,000 characters (139) were dropped because of API token limits (p.275, fn. 8).
Topic labels are checked only by the 400-speech intruder task; the LDA comparison is conceptual and cited, not estimated in this paper.
GPT-4 showed little or no improvement over GPT-3 on the ideology and sentiment tasks, so the best-model choice is not settled across tasks (p.273, lines 438-440).
measures: Sentiment: first principal component of the Positive/Negative/Neutral next-word probability vector per tweet, compared with a 7-point author-coded score from -1 to +1 (Fleiss kappa 0.72).
Tone: continuous score from the one-shot ad-tone prompt probability vector, compared with expert ratings of the 935 ads.
Ideology: per-sentence score P(Conservative) minus P(Liberal), averaged to economic and social passage means per manifesto; compared with expert scores (rho 0.92 economic, 0.8 social).
Topic: count and share of speeches mentioning each virtue label (and synonyms), by party; difference in percentage points.
Classification accuracy: share of tweets whose predicted negative/positive sign matches the author label (88.4% for GPT-3).
Calibration: share of posts with a single-label probability above 99 percent (GPT-4).

summary_md:
Ornstein, Blasingame and Truscott (PSRM 2025, DOI 10.1017/psrm.2024.64) test few-shot prompts to GPT-3 and GPT-4 on four political text tasks. The tasks are sentiment in 945 SCOTUS tweets, tone in 935 campaign ads, ideology in 18,263 sentences from UK manifestos, and virtue-topic labels for 9,565 House one-minute speeches. On the tweets, GPT-3 got 88.4% of negative/positive signs right, against 64.3% for TweetNLP, 57.7% for Naive Bayes and 38.3% for the best dictionary. On ideology, LLM scores correlate with expert scores at rho 0.92 (economic) and 0.80 (social) across the 18 manifestos. LLM topic labels beat three random intruders in 80% of 400 blinded checks, where chance is 25%. Costs dropped about 1000-fold compared with crowd coding.

Three method points matter more than the headline numbers:
- Continuous measures are built from the label probability vector, not the argmax label.
- GPT-4, tuned with human feedback (RLHF), is overconfident. For over 70% of posts it put more than 99% on one label, and it chose Neutral more often than the human coders.
- Validation runs in three steps: tune the prompt on one hand-labelled set, check it on a second, then apply.

The authors also warn that the GPT-3 models they used were retired in January 2024, so the results cannot be reproduced.

For Paul's system, the paper does not bear on networks, money or allocation. It bears on the stance and text layer. Melange already supplies outside context in the prompt for its Claude stance rater, and it caches LLM outputs by model. The gaps are elsewhere:
- run_stage5.R throws away DEBATE's per-label probabilities and keeps only a sign, which is then multiplied by dictionary intensity.
- The Claude rater reports a confidence it states itself, not a calibrated probability.
- Regex topic routing has never been checked against human labels.
- The tweet gold queue puts the model's labels next to the human gold columns.

The paper measures sentiment toward court rulings, not stance toward a target, so its accuracy figures should not be read as an expected accuracy for CU stance.

bearings.paper_claim: Continuous measures built from the label probability vector: per-sentence P(Conservative) minus P(Liberal), averaged per manifesto, gives rho 0.92 (economic) and 0.80 (social) across 18 UK manifestos with GPT-3. Tweet sentiment uses the first principal component of the positive/negative/neutral probability vector.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.1 p.267-268 (PCA of probability vector, lines 276-280); Section 3.3 p.273 (rho 0.92 and 0.8, Figure 6, lines 441-445)
bearings.system_side: run_stage5.R:143 sets press_value = final_sign x intensity, where intensity is abs(lsd_net_norm) by default (line 141). final_sign is the bill sign or stance_sign, which is the argmax of DEBATE (run_stage5.R:140; stage5_debate.py:77-82). run_stage5.R:9 is a comment only. p_support, p_oppose and p_neutral are kept as columns (run_stage5.R:98,166) and do not enter press_value.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper evidence uses GPT-3 next-token probabilities on a few-shot prompt, not DEBATE NLI entailment scores. DEBATE runs with multi_label=True (stage5_debate.py:65), so its three scores are independent and do not sum to 1. A p_support minus p_oppose contrast is a different object and would need a pre-registered single look on the 760-row press gold. Remains UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers and PCA/contrast description checked against the text and confirmed. Code cite for the press_value formula corrected from :9 (a comment) to :143. The p_* columns claim is accurate. Downstream effect is not traced here.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#press_value aggregate and human-label overlay|press_value aggregate and human-label overlay]]

bearings.paper_claim: Tweets whose meaning depends on outside political context are misread unless the prompt supplies that context. The Masterpiece sentiment prompt included a preamble on the ruling and six few-shot examples, and GPT-3 got the sign right on 88.4 percent of 945 tweets.
bearings.system_side: The system described is claude_stance.py, not DEBATE. Its SYSTEM prompt (lines 19-23) carries a credit-union policy map and tells the model to judge by the member position on the underlying issue, not by the words credit union. Its docstring (lines 5-8) names it the pre-labeller and the third member of the ensemble, with the Credit Card Competition Act example.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper task is sentiment toward a court ruling, not stance toward an interest, so the paper gives no accuracy figure for CU stance. The paper used six few-shot examples; claude_stance.py is zero-shot with a policy map. The supported point is the design choice of supplying context in the prompt.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claim verified at p.267-268. The component ID names the DEBATE classifier, but the system_side describes the Claude rater, so the bearing belongs to the Claude rater component. Context-in-prompt design is supported.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader|Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader]]

bearings.paper_claim: GPT-4, tuned with RLHF, is poorly calibrated and overconfident. For over 70 percent of its posts it gave one label more than 99 percent probability, and it chose Neutral more often than the authors. GPT-4 was slightly worse than GPT-3 on sentiment and little or no better on ideology. Section 4 says newer RLHF models frequently underperform on classification and scaling tasks, and the latest model is not always the best.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.1 p.268 (lines 288-296); Section 3.3 p.273 (lines 438-440); Section 4 p.278 (lines 589-597)
bearings.system_side: claude_stance.py asks for a self-stated confidence from 0 to 1 in its JSON reply (line 25) and defaults to claude-sonnet-4-6 (line 32). A call that fails all 4 attempts stays neutral with confidence 0.0 and reason ERR (lines 80, 95-97). An unrecognised label is set to neutral (lines 89-91), but the stated confidence is still read at line 92, so it is not reset to 0.0.
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are GPT-3 and GPT-4 results, not Claude results. The module requests no token log-probabilities (none found in the file), so the paper probability-vector method cannot be applied as written. claude_conf is a self-stated number, not a calibrated probability. Neutral rows created by ERR should be counted apart from model-chosen neutral rows. No DEBATE-vs-Claude agreement figure was located in the sources checked.
bearings.verifier_note: Calibration figures and page cites confirmed. Claim that unrecognised labels get confidence 0.0 is wrong (line 92 keeps the stated value). The 'newer models did not improve on any task' wording overstates the paper, so it is restated. The 87.2 percent agreement figure is not supported by sources read and is removed. Anthropic log-probability claim is restated from the code only.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader|Fine-tuned Political DEBATE NLI stance reader]]

bearings.paper_claim: Dictionary methods lose badly when meaning depends on context. The best dictionary the authors could build got 38.3 percent of tweet signs right, against 88.4 percent for GPT-3. Of 5332 speeches containing honor, GPT-3 labels only 145 as praising honor.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.1 p.268 (lines 282-286); Section 3.4 p.276 (lines 544-549)
bearings.system_side: LSD2015 is used only for intensity. run_stage5.R:141 takes abs(lsd_net_norm) by default, or lsd_charge when CU_S5_INTENSITY=charge, and line 143 multiplies it by final_sign. stage5_lsd.R (header lines 10-15) matches and removes negation phrases before counting. Direction in run_stage5.R comes from the DEBATE stance with bill-sign and human-label overrides (lines 139-140), not from the Claude rater.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper dictionary is the authors own construction, not LSD2015, and the paper did not test intensity. Intensity inherits the context blindness the paper describes (ceremonial or quoted language reads as heated). Whether LSD intensity tracks human-coded intensity is untested.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers and page cites confirmed. The cited stage5_debate.py:11-12 is a docstring; the LSD code is in stage5_lsd.R. The statement that direction also comes from the Claude reader is not supported by run_stage5.R and is removed.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity|Lexicoder LSD2015 tone intensity]]

bearings.paper_claim: LLM topic labels can be checked with an optimal-label task. In 400 speeches a blinded coder picked the GPT-3 label over three random intruders 80 percent of the time, against 25 percent chance. Keyword presence overcounts: 5332 speeches contain honor, but only 145 are labelled as praising it.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.4 p.276 (lines 534-549)
bearings.system_side: Release and post categories come from regex keyword maps (CATKW = MR.RAW_PATTERNS at build_media_blend.py:50). No human-label check of those regex tags was found in the files read. Downstream use (media blend, press category weights) was not traced.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper labels are open-ended virtue labels for 2013-2014 House speeches; Melange uses fixed CU policy categories on releases and posts. The intruder protocol transfers as a measurement check on existing regex tags. Adopting LLM-assigned categories would be a separate decision. The R scraper CATEGORIES regex was not opened.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers confirmed. The claim that the categories drive the media blend and the press category weights was not traced and is removed from the verified text. The protocol suggestion is a fair design implication.

bearings.paper_claim: The recommended validation has three steps: hand-label a small set to design the prompt, validate on a second hand-labelled set (by the team or crowd coders) for strong correlation with ground truth, then apply. Crowd workers increasingly use LLMs (Veselovsky et al. 2023), which threatens crowd-code independence.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4 p.277 (lines 567-575); Veselovsky point in Section 3.2 p.270-271 (lines 335-343)
bearings.system_side: build_tweet_gold_queue.py writes model_stance and model_margin into the same rows as the human gold_* columns (lines 92-96). The api_* columns are written as blank placeholders reserved for an optional pre-label pass (line 18 and lines 92-96). Low-margin (Q_LOWMARGIN) and anti-bank (Q_ANTIBANK) slices are oversampled (lines 25-27).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper does not test anchoring on pre-labels, so this is a design implication, not a measured effect. If a labeller sees model_stance, agreement with gold partly measures agreement with the model. Oversampled hard slices make these accuracies incomparable with the paper random-sample 88.4 percent.
bearings.verifier_note: Oversampling and column structure confirmed. The api_* block is blank at write time, not a populated pre-label block. The Veselovsky point sits in Section 3.2, not Section 4. Treating hand labels as the independent criterion is an interpretation of the paper recommendation.

bearings.paper_claim: Results from closed, vendor-served models can become impossible to reproduce. The GPT-3 models behind the paper results were removed from the public-facing API in January 2024.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4 p.278 (lines 598-605)
bearings.system_side: member_reference_layer.py records which model scored each cached row (_cache_models, lines 258-265) and stores resp.model and resp.id with each classification (line 306). agency_communion_llm.py keeps a separate cache file per model (CACHE path, lines 24-28), so instruments do not mix.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Caching keeps outputs auditable after a model is retired, but does not regenerate them; a re-score on a successor model is a new instrument. The warning applies because both layers call Anthropic-served models. The component label is a weak fit for LLM caching and should name the member-reference and persona LLM layers.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claim and date confirmed at p.278. Code side confirmed for per-model caching and response metadata. The display-only or low-weight status of both layers was not checked.

bearings.paper_claim: Few-shot LLM classification can match or beat crowd and expert coding, but results depend heavily on prompt design and need checks against hand labels the prompt was not tuned on.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.264; Section 4 p.277-278
bearings.system_side: agency_communion_llm.py uses a few-shot codebook with strong (1.0) and weak (0.5) cue conditions (docstring lines 5-7; method string near lines 238-239) and classifies sentence-level cues. The 18/18 functional gate, the party signature, and the absence of held-out human-gold accuracy were not verified. PERSONA_W was not found in agency_communion_llm.py, so its definition lives elsewhere.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper validates document-level measures against expert and crowd codes; the cues here are sentence-level and aggregated per member. A paper-style check would need a hand-coded cue sample that was not used to write the codebook. PERSONA_W 0.30 is an owner ruling and is not changed by this review.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claim holds as a general statement. Code side verified only for the codebook and the strong/weak weights. The validation status and PERSONA_W value were not checked, so no claim about them is confirmed.

The Claude stance rater has no calibrated probabilities: its confidence is stated by the model in its JSON reply, and API errors silently become neutral at confidence 0 (claude_stance.py:80,89-91).
The regex category router (CATKW, build_media_blend.py:50) has no human-label validation. The paper's 400-item intruder task is a ready, cheap protocol for this.

Gold queues put model_stance and api_* pre-labels next to the gold_* columns (build_tweet_gold_queue.py:92-96). Nothing records whether gold labelling was blind to the model, so the assumption that gold is independent of the pipeline is untested.
No plan exists for retiring a model. The caches keep outputs, but no documented rule says how a successor model's scores are bridged or re-validated before they replace cached ones.
flags: The paper measures SENTIMENT toward SCOTUS rulings, not target-specific STANCE. The brain separates sentiment from stance, so do not quote the 88.4% figure as an expected accuracy for CU stance.
The paper's numbers come from GPT-3 and GPT-4 (2023-2024 API), and GPT-3 was retired in January 2024. Its figures cannot be reproduced and say nothing directly about Claude or DEBATE.

The cost figures ($0.60 vs $565.20; $2.50 vs about $3,226.70) are OpenAI prices from that period. They describe the window and denominator stated in the paper (935 ads; 18,263 sentences), not Melange's current costs.

Any re-scoring proposed here (a probability-contrast stance, LLM categories) is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). Any replacement of a live reader needs a pre-registered single look against held-out gold.
Possible conflict with the gold-set assumption that gold labels are independent of the pipeline: the tweet gold queue shows model outputs next to the gold columns.
Nothing in the paper touches the rejected SNA proposals, LDA edges, reciprocity, graph-rank or influence wording.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations on this paper. His position on the stance components endorses LLM and transformer extraction (Kim J. 2025, Birkenmaier and Lechner 2025) and calls SVM baselines outdated. The paper broadly agrees: GPT-3 beat a fine-tuned RoBERTa (TweetNLP) and Naive Bayes on tweet sentiment. It adds two cautions his notes lack. First, newer RLHF models (GPT-4) were overconfident and no better. Second, every LLM measure needs separate hand-labelled validation. Paul's preference is partly stale against the system's own record: on the member-grouped held-out test, LinearSVC on TF-IDF scored 83.9%, against 0.757 reported for the transformer. The paper's 88.4% is a sentiment task, not CU stance. His noted weakness, that ambiguous statements are hard to untangle, matches the paper's finding that context-dependent items fail unless the prompt supplies context. The system's Claude rater already supplies that context.

related.why: Both papers use few-shot LLM coding checked against human labels. The persona channel code cites Birkenmaier and Lechner cue prompting (agency_communion_llm.py docstring). Ornstein does not cite Birkenmaier, and the Krippendorff-alpha role is not verified here.

Kim and Ornstein both apply few-shot GPT-class labelling to political text. Ornstein documents GPT-4 overconfidence on sentiment. Ornstein does not cite Kim. The 96.9 percent figure appears in the Kim item file but was not checked against Kim text.

Khan et al. compare fine-tuned RoBERTa with classical models for political tweet stance. Ornstein uses TweetNLP (a RoBERTa model) as the sentiment baseline that GPT-3 beats, 88.4 vs 64.3 percent. The tasks differ: Khan is stance, Ornstein is sentiment.

Rice and Zorn build corpus-specific dictionaries. Ornstein does not cite them and does not test corpus-specific dictionaries. Ornstein shows a general dictionary at 38.3 percent against GPT-3 at 88.4 percent on tweet sentiment, which bears on dictionary validity.

Haselmayer and Jenny combine a dictionary with crowd coding. Ornstein benchmarks LLM coding against crowd coding alone (Carlson and Montgomery 2017; Benoit et al. 2016), reporting about a 1000-fold cost reduction for 935 ad codings. The dictionary-plus-crowd route is not tested.
Both apply LLMs to political stance and sentiment classification. Dai adds logic-tensor constraints; Ornstein uses few-shot prompts with probability-vector outputs. Ornstein does not cite Dai.

extraction.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Voter Dynamics
extraction.year: Not printed in the text (metadata hint says 2025; latest cited reference is 2024, Palermo et al.)
extraction.venue: Preprint submitted to Elsevier (29 pages). No journal named in the text. Affiliations: Xiamen University of Technology (Cai); University of Southampton (Gerding, Brede).
extraction.document_type: Preprint manuscript (simulation and mean-field analysis; not empirical)
extraction.coverage: Read all 2506 lines of the text file in three chunks (lines 1-955, 956-1755, 1756-2506), covering abstract, introduction, Sections 2-5, Appendices A-E, acknowledgements and references. Nothing omitted. Paul markup: none supplied (the task listed no markup files), so paul_markup is empty. Coverage is complete for the text as extracted; figure content is read only from axis labels and captions.
extraction.research_question: How do the timing and distribution of a time-limited, budget-constrained influence campaign shape the final vote share in a voter model, and how does network degree heterogeneity change the optimal campaign timing? Two settings: (1) one controller (A) against a constant, fixed opponent (B); (2) two controllers choosing start times simultaneously in a zero-sum game (paper Sections 1, 2, abstract p.1).
extraction.theory: Non-progressive voter model (reversible opinion changes; Masuda 2015) with heterogeneous mean-field theory and relaxation-time analysis (Son et al. 2008). Degree heterogeneity drives timescales. Competitive timing and budget allocation are analysed with interior-point optimization, stochastic hill climbing, and minimax-based iterative search for Nash equilibria in a zero-sum game. Partial zealotry (Masuda et al. 2010; Moreno et al. 2020) adds agent heterogeneity. Authors contrast their smooth zealotry with latency models (Palermo et al. 2024).
extraction.data:
Simulated and real networks, no empirical opinion or vote-outcome data.
(a) Synthetic configuration-model scale-free networks. Main experiments: N = 10^4 nodes, target mean degree 10 (realized 10.5), degree exponent lambda in [1.6, 5], k_max = sqrt(N) (p.11, p.25). Individual-optimization experiments: N = 10^2, mean degree 6, k_max = 30, 10 realizations (p.17, p.25). Complete-network zealotry experiment: N = 10^2 (p.26). Each figure reports 100 or 10 realizations (see captions).
(b) Real networks, Table 1 (p.11): Congress votes N=219, 764 edges, mean degree 7.0, lambda about 1.9 (text: mentions between US politicians with supportive or opposing edges). Facebook N=3862, 87324 edges, mean degree 45.2, lambda about 1.6 (users affiliated with one corporation). Advogato N=6541, 51127 edges, mean degree 15.6, lambda about 1.7 (trust network). Wikipedia Elections N=7118, 103689 edges, mean degree 29.1, lambda about 1.5 (positive/negative votes between users; these are Wikipedia admin-style votes, not political elections). Twitter N=22322, 31823 edges, mean degree 2.9, lambda about 4.3 (following network).
Unit of analysis: individual node (agent). Time: simulated horizons T=16 (short) and T=256 (long), dimensionless model time, not calendar periods. Initial opinion share 0.5 for all nodes (or 0 in some experiments, p.18, p.26); one illustrative example uses S_A(0)=0.55 with N=10^4, T=30 (p.5).
extraction.method:
Analytical plus numerical simulation.
- Model (Eq. 1, p.4): each node's opinion-A probability x_i(t) evolves under neighbour influence and two controllers with time-varying gains a_i(t), b_i(t). Budget constraints sum of integrals <= b_A, b_B (p.3-4). Vote share S_A(T) = mean of x_i(T) (Eq. 2).
- Constant-opponent, uniform start (Sec 2.1, Eq. 3-5): A's gain is 0 until t_a, then b_A/((T-t_a)N); B's gain is constant b_B/(TN). Optimal t_a solved by interior-point method (p.5).
- Individual optimization (Sec 2.2, Eq. 6-7): each node has its own start time and budget; stochastic hill climbing (Algorithm 1, p.7), with L_max = N^2 iterations (p.26). Budget moves between nodes keep the total fixed.
- Heterogeneity extension (Sec 2.2.1, Eq. 8): partial zealots with probability q_i of resisting adoption of A when holding B.
- Game (Sec 2.3, Eq. 9; Algorithm 2, p.8): simultaneous choice of start times t_a, t_b; iterative alternating best responses (A maximizes, B minimizes S_A(T)) with step size mu = 1/i, stopping threshold 1e-9 (p.8).
- Mean-field (Sec 3, Eq. 10-11, derived in App. B): nodes grouped by degree k; closed-form x_k(t) and S_A(t).
- Relaxation times (Eq. 12-14, 19): normalized order parameter r_k(t); tau_relax,k and tau_relax as degree-weighted averages; l-percentage relaxation time tau^l.
- Taylor expansion (Eq. 15-18) to second order in 1/k, assuming (a_k+b_k)/k << 1.
- Numerical integration: 4th-order Runge-Kutta, time step 0.01 (p.11).
- Real-network experiments: Table 2 compares optimized t_a with t_a=0 at T in {16, 256} and b_A/b_B in {0.1, 1, 10}.
- Appendix A: single-node case with fully flexible allocation via calculus of variations (Eq. 20-30), yielding a transcendental equation for start time.
extraction.identification: None in a causal sense; model-based simulation. Mean-field and Taylor predictions are validated against Runge-Kutta integration (Fig. 2, 3, 4c-f; p.11-16). Optimality of the start time is checked by a convex vote-share peak (Fig. 4c-d, p.15-16). Within-model comparison is optimized start versus t_a=0 (Table 2, p.18).
extraction.scope: Population: abstract simulated networks (configuration model) and five public network datasets; no sampled human population. Era: none stated. Opinions: binary (A or B), simple contagion, unit link weights, complete knowledge of network topology assumed (p.22-23). Applications named as motivation only (marketing, politics, public health; p.1-2, p.22); no application-specific calibration or validation is reported.

key_findings.finding: Constant-opponent, uniform start: optimal strategy is to delay. The controller lets the opponent dominate early, reserves budget, and then increases allocation sharply near the deadline.
key_findings.location: Sec 4.3.1, p.16-17; Fig. 5a; Sec 1 p.3 (main finding i)
key_findings.numbers: Example budgets: N=10^4, T=30, b_A=1.5e4, b_B=1.2e4; S_A(0)=0.55 (p.5). Optimal control time (T - t_a) plotted for T in {1,...,512} (Fig. 5a).

key_findings.finding: Network heterogeneity shifts optimal timing with horizon. For short horizons, highly heterogeneous networks (low lambda) should start later; for long horizons they should start earlier.
key_findings.location: Sec 4.3.1, p.16-17; Sec 1 p.3 (main finding i)
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative pattern from Fig. 5a (T=16 vs T=256 curves). Fig. 4e: at T=16 the degree of equilibrium l never exceeds 0.82 (p.16).

key_findings.finding: Relaxation time increases with node degree; higher-degree nodes equilibrate more slowly. Mean-field and Taylor estimates track Runge-Kutta.
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 2(a) relaxation time on a y-axis of about 52-56 across degree 2-92 (N=10^4, mean degree 10.5, lambda=1.6, 100 realizations). Uniform targeting: tau_relax,k approximately independent of initial state (p.10).

key_findings.finding: More heterogeneous networks (lower lambda) have longer overall equilibration times, driven by high-degree nodes.
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 2(b) x-axis lambda in [1.6, 5]; y-axis tau_relax about 6.35-6.45. Text: more heterogeneous networks have longer timescales (quoted).

key_findings.finding: Degree of equilibrium l reverses the ranking of relaxation times. At low l, less heterogeneous networks (high lambda) take longer; near equilibrium, more heterogeneous networks take longer. Early changes are driven by low-degree nodes; late changes by high-degree nodes.
key_findings.numbers: Fig. 3 uses N=10^4, mean degree 10.5, lambda=1.6 and 5, 100 realizations. Low/high degree split at 80%/20% (Pareto). Fig. 3(a) tau^l axis about 1-6 (inset 5-6.5 near equilibrium).

key_findings.numbers: Congress votes T=16: b_A/b_B=1 gives opt t_a 12.533, S_A 0.705 vs 0.500 at t_a=0; b_A/b_B=0.1 gives 14.730, 0.248 vs 0.117; b_A/b_B=10 gives 10.476, 0.958 vs 0.909. key_findings.finding: Budget advantage means earlier start. A controller with more budget relative to its rival starts influence earlier; a disadvantaged controller starts later.

key_findings.numbers: Congress votes T=16: opt t_a falls from 14.730 (ratio 0.1) to 10.476 (ratio 10). Fig. 5b fixes T=16 with optimal start 9-15 across lambda and ratio 0.01-100 (axis).

key_findings.numbers: N=10^4, mean degree 10.5, T=16, b_B=N*T, b_A=10*b_B, 100 realizations per Fig. 8 setup (text: 'Calculations based on N=10^4'). Three stages: no control; first mover; both control.

key_findings.finding: Analytical single-node result: with fully flexible control against a constant opponent, the optimal start time satisfies a transcendental equation; a larger budget ratio pushes the start earlier.

limitations: Binary opinions and simple contagion only; complex contagion and multi-state opinion models are not studied (p.22).
Assumes complete knowledge of network topology and of the opponent's strategy; partial visibility and uncertain opponent behaviour are flagged as future work (p.22-23).

Mean-field analysis assumes degree-uncorrelated networks (p.9); its accuracy is validated only on configuration-model networks and not on the five real datasets (no mean-field check reported for Table 2).
Taylor expansion valid only when (a_k+b_k)/k is small (p.10).
Individual optimization restricted to N=10^2 for computational reasons; absolute improvements described as very small (p.17-18).

Stochastic hill climbing and the iterative Nash algorithm are numerical heuristics; the text reports no optimality guarantee (p.7-8). Nash equilibria are approximated, not solved in closed form (p.8).
Individual optimization is not analysed in the game-theoretic setting because gains are small (p.22).
Integer k_min forces realized mean degree to deviate from target (target 10 gives 10.5) (p.25).
Degree exponent lower bound 1.6 chosen because lower values fail the k_min constraint (p.25).

Real datasets are not election outcome or lobbying data: Congress votes are mentions/support-oppose edges, Wikipedia Elections are user-to-user votes, Facebook and Twitter are social graphs. No validation against observed vote shares is reported.
Time horizons are abstract model units; no calendar mapping is given beyond the illustrative 30-day example (p.5).

summary_md:
Cai, Gerding and Brede study a time-limited, budget-constrained influence campaign in a non-progressive voter model, where opinions can flip back. They use heterogeneous mean-field theory, relaxation-time analysis, hill climbing and an iterative minimax search for Nash start times. Every result is a simulation on configuration-model scale-free graphs or on five public graphs. The paper uses no observed votes, lobbying or money data.

Findings. Against a fixed opponent, the best strategy is to hold budget back and spend it late. Across all datasets, horizons and budget ratios in Table 2, an optimized start beat starting at t=0. One example is the 'Congress votes' mentions graph at T=16 with equal budgets: vote share 0.705 against 0.500. A richer controller starts earlier: on that graph the optimal start falls from 14.73 at budget ratio 0.1 to 10.48 at ratio 10. High-degree nodes take longer to settle, so on a short horizon the outcome stays far from equilibrium (degree of equilibrium never above 0.82 at T=16). In the two-controller game the side with more budget moves first, and the second mover can only offset its lead, not overtake it. Small budgets go to low-degree nodes. Partial zealots get fewer resources than normal agents.

Why it matters here. Melange's money engines have no time dimension at all. The flip model's pflip = a/(a+b) is a stationary share ratio with no time term, the optimizer allocates dollars with no timing, and the competitive cascades let a member who has been reached stay that colour. The paper is the clearest formal case in the vault that timing and reversibility change who wins under a fixed budget. Its evidence is abstract: model time units, unit edge weights, full knowledge of the network, and no calibration to any real campaign. Read it as a design critique and a source of hypotheses. It does not validate or refute any Melange constant, and any agent analysis built on it stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Vote share at a finite horizon depends on when each controller starts and on degree heterogeneity. At T=16 (dimensionless model time, unit-weight graphs) the degree of equilibrium l never exceeds 0.82 and high-degree nodes relax more slowly. An optimized start beats t_a=0 in all 30 rows of Table 2 (5 real networks, T in {16, 256}, budget ratio in {0.1, 1, 10}). Congress votes network, T=16, budget ratio 1: S_A 0.705 vs 0.500 (model output, not observed votes).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.2 p.11-16 (text around Fig 4e); Sec 4.3.1 Table 2 p.18
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), where a and b are each a saturating money pull plus a party-weighted proximity term. It is a static, time-free share with no horizon, no start time and no relaxation lag.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Structural parallel only: both are ratios of competing pulls. Magnitudes do not transfer, since paper time is dimensionless, edges have unit weight and opinions are binary simple contagion. The paper shows that an equilibrium-share form omits timing, not that pflip is miscalibrated.
bearings.verifier_note: Table 2 (30 rows) and text lines 1385-1410 checked; every optimized vote share exceeds its t_a=0 baseline. The pflip formula and docstring match the code. Claim holds. Any quoted figure should name the window (T, dimensionless) and denominator (N=10^4 synthetic; N for Table 1 real networks).

bearings.paper_claim: With the budget fixed, choosing a start time raises final vote share over spending from t=0 (Table 2, constant-opponent setting). For N=100 networks, per-node start times and budgets raise vote share further: the relative gain is large at small budget ratios but small in absolute terms (Fig 6a relative axis 1.00 to 1.25). A resource-limited controller starts later and a resource-rich one starts earlier (abstract; Sec 4.3.1). Under the uniform-start formula (Eq 3-5) the controller spends its budget over a short late window; the paper does not prescribe this as a rule.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.1; Sec 2.1 Eq 3-5 p.4-5; Sec 4.3.1 Table 2 p.18; Sec 4.3.2 Fig 6 p.17-18
bearings.system_side: optimize.py docstring describes a lazy greedy allocator with a Golovin-Krause bound kept as a diagnostic. Defaults are a 2.5M pot in 500 increments with a 10k per-candidate cap (PMAX). It allocates amounts per member with no start time or spending schedule; the objective is time-free winnability.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only as a hypothesis. PAC dollars cannot be withdrawn, FEC per-cycle limits bind, and the paper's continuous gain a_i(t) has no clear counterpart in lump-sum contributions. The paper's large relative gain at small budgets means the per-node result should not be read as uniformly small. Untested on legislators.
bearings.verifier_note: Core claims hold (Table 2, Fig 6 axis labels, abstract). The rewrite adds the large relative gain at small budget ratios, which the bearing omitted. The spend-near-deadline wording is a reading of Eq 3-5, not a paper statement. The name CELF does not appear in the docstring; the code is described as lazy greedy. Appendix A Eq 30 was not re-derived.

bearings.paper_claim: Two settings are mixed here. The optimal start for Congress votes at T=16 falls from 14.730 at budget ratio 0.1 to 10.476 at ratio 10 (Table 2, constant-opponent setting, fixed opponent starting at 0). In the two-controller Nash game the controller with the larger budget moves first, and the second mover can only buffer the first mover's gain, never exceed its vote share (Sec 4.3.4, stage 3, p.21-22). Fig 9b shows per-node resource per unit time rising with the budget advantage.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.3.1 Table 2 p.18; Sec 4.3.4 Fig 8-9 p.19-22
bearings.system_side: The head-to-head panel solves CU share against competitor share in closed form for the baseline odds. It reports that CU money alone cannot fully offset when the required money ratio q is at least 1. The solve uses the CU-to-competitor money ratio at one instant, with no sequencing.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's statement that a disadvantaged controller can offset but not overtake agrees in spirit with the cannot-offset message. The claim that a disadvantaged side does better by delaying has no counterpart in a static break-even, and it rests on the paper's abstract and simulations only. Transfer would need a model of within-cycle spending order, which the system lacks.
bearings.verifier_note: The 14.730, 10.476, 0.705 and 0.500 values match Table 2, but Table 2 is the constant-opponent setting, not the game; the original bearing attributed them to the game. The game statement is qualitative. The code description checks out. Fig 9b per-node axis values were not verified against the figure image.

bearings.paper_claim: Competitive influence is analysed in a non-progressive voter model with reversible opinions, where the opponent is a strategic controller choosing its own start time at a Nash equilibrium (Eq 9, Algorithm 2 p.8; Fig 8 p.19-20). extraction.title: An Improved D* Lite-Based Dynamic Route Planning Algorithm for Ships in Arctic Waters
extraction.venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering, 12, 2323 (MDPI, Basel); published 18 Dec 2024
extraction.document_type: Journal article: algorithm design plus simulation benchmark (open access, CC BY 4.0)
extraction.coverage: Full text read (all 1,126 extracted lines, pp. 1-22, including references and disclaimer). Metadata hint confirmed: title, year, venue, DOI correct. No Paul markup files were supplied (task listed none). Topical fit to the vault is low: the paper covers graph-search path planning only. It has no content on lobbying, elections, turnout, persuasion, legislators, text measurement, or social networks, beyond the general fact that the graph is a grid.
extraction.research_question: How can D* Lite dynamic replanning be made cheap enough for real-time ship routing in Arctic waters, where ice conditions change over large areas, while keeping route distance and average risk close to full re-planning? The authors set the goal as cutting node updates and planning time without changing the heuristic.
extraction.theory: No social-science theory. The basis is graph-search path planning: incremental replanning from LPA* and D* (Koenig and Likhachev 2002, ref. 26), a risk-weighted movement cost (cost = delta*r + d, Eq. 12), and a ship-specific icebreaking limit (maximum continuous ice-breaking thickness) used in place of ice-class rules.
extraction.data: Sea ice thickness and related ice data from CryoSat-2 (European Space Agency), stated in Sec. 4 (data availability: NSIDC, accessed 29 April 2024). Study area 55-90 degrees N, grid 448 x 304 cells at 25 km x 25 km. Unit: grid cell (node) and route update. Two simulated voyages, one per period: freezing (October 2023 dataset, 26 route updates) and melting (mid-April to mid-May 2023, 24 route updates). No ship sample. Ship parameters are a single hypothetical vessel with icebreaking thickness 1.2 m (freezing) or 2.8 m (melting), risk threshold 1, and a fixed update distance of 8 grid units per update. Text says this is "approximately 432 nautical miles", which does not match the stated grid resolution (see limitations).
extraction.scope: Population: one Arctic region, two ice periods (freezing October 2023; melting April-May 2023), one ship type parameterized by icebreaking thickness and safety coefficient. Institution: Shanghai Maritime University (Merchant Marine College). Era: 2023 ice data, paper published Dec 2024. Speed differences by ice condition are excluded (Sec. 4, p. 13).
extraction.method: Improved D* Lite with three modified rules. (1) Local update (Sec. 2.2, Eq. 5, Algorithm 1): a node that becomes an obstacle takes its cost from the old data, and a node that becomes navigable takes its cost from the new data, so updates do not spread through the whole map. (2) Path extraction (Sec. 2.3, Eq. 6, Algorithm 2): the next node is the unexplored successor minimizing c + g, which avoids deadlocks at the boundary of updated regions. (3) Path optimization (Sec. 2.4, Eqs. 7-9): shortcut any segment where the direct connection costs less and has no obstacles. Risk r = h x C / Icemax (Eq. 10); cost = delta*r + d (Eq. 12); average route risk R = sum(r_i d_i)/sum(d_i) (Eq. 13). Non-navigable cells are land, cells with average ice thickness above Icemax, and cells with r above the threshold (Sec. 3.1). Benchmarks: global re-planning every update, and the original D* Lite. All three run on identical ice snapshots and ship positions.
extraction.identification_strategy: None. This is a simulation benchmark, not a causal design. Validity rests on comparing against global re-planning, treated as optimal under the same heuristic (Sec. 4.1, p. 14-15), and against the original D* Lite. Parameter effects (Icemax, delta) are shown only by re-running the same voyage with different settings (Sec. 4.3, Table 5).

key_findings.finding: Freezing period, improved vs original D* Lite: nodes updated fell by 34.9% (18,468 vs 28,351); planning time fell by 46.2% (924 s vs 1,720 s). Voyage distance 2,558.7 vs 2,561.4 n mi; average risk identical at 0.076.
Freezing period, improved vs global re-planning: nodes updated fell 74.6% and planning time fell 72.7%. Route quality matched global re-planning on risk, with distance within about 0.1%.
Melting period, improved vs original D* Lite: nodes updated fell 79.5% and planning time fell 85.7%. Voyage distance 2,419.1 vs 2,418.1 n mi; risk identical at 0.615.
Melting period, improved vs global re-planning: nodes updated fell 85.3% and planning time fell 86.7%.

Sensitivity, freezing period: raising Icemax from 1.0 to 1.4 m shortens the route (2,654.5 to 2,459.9 n mi) and raises average risk (0.002 to 0.113). Raising delta from 1 to 3 at 1.2 m lengthens the route (2,558.7 to 2,645.5 n mi) and lowers risk (0.076 to 0.039).

Sensitivity, melting period: delta 1 to 3 at 2.8 m lengthens the route (2,419.1 to 2,644.1 n mi) and lowers risk (0.615 to 0.468). Risk does not fall monotonically with Icemax: at delta 1 it is 0.625, 0.631, 0.615 for 2.4, 2.6, 2.8 m.
Safety coefficient delta = 3 is adopted as sufficient on the basis of unpublished simulations: higher values did not change route outcomes much.

key_findings.finding: Discussion, single illustrative map (Icemax 0.8 m, PC-6-equivalent): the POLARIS-based route crosses non-navigable cells, while the proposed risk formula routes around them. Qualitative only, no numbers.

summary_md:
Xu et al. (2024) change D* Lite so that a ship's route can be re-planned cheaply as Arctic ice changes. The test grid is 448 x 304 cells at 25 km. They make three changes: (1) a local-update rule, where a cell that becomes blocked keeps its old cost and a cell that opens takes its new cost, so changes don't spread across the whole map; (2) a path-extraction rule that picks the unexplored successor with the lowest c+g, which avoids deadlocks at the edge of updated regions; (3) shortcut smoothing. Cost is a weighted sum, delta*risk + distance.

Compared with the original D* Lite, nodes updated fell 34.9% in the freezing period (18,468 vs 28,351) and 79.5% in the melting period. Planning time fell 46% and 86%. Route length stayed within about 0.1%, and average risk was unchanged. Raising delta trades length for risk (freezing period: R 0.076 to 0.039, distance +3.4%). Each period is one simulated voyage, with no variance and no hardware stated. Some numbers in the text don't match the tables: 8 cells x 25 km is about 108 n mi, not 432, and the 0.07% error figure can't be reproduced.

For Paul's systems the paper is narrow. None of the router code (fec/) has D* Lite or LPA*. The gains need large graphs where repeated queries see small, local changes. The 533-node cosponsor graph is too small for incremental replanning to matter, and the staffer router serves many different origin/target pairs. Its approximate local update would also break Paul's 2026-10-03 rule that staffer routes must be exactly optimal. The paper's sharpest use is diagnostic. Its warning that extracting a path from stale cost-to-goal values can deadlock describes the dashboard's buildPath "member dropped" mode: distToTarget ignores dropped members, but tracePath skips them, so the chain labelled "PROVABLY-OPTIMAL" is not optimal once someone is dropped (UNVERIFIED, read from the code but not run). The paper also shows that scenario.py's D* Lite citation claims a reuse of earlier work that the code doesn't do.

Its fix (Eq. 6, Algorithm 2) picks the unexplored successor minimizing passage cost plus g and excludes explored nodes. The 18,468 vs 28,351 freezing node counts compare the whole improved method (local update plus extraction plus path optimization) with the original D* Lite, not Eq. 6 alone. The paper does not say the g values are out of date or made consistent with the change.

When members are dropped, dT still counts routes through them, so the greedy trace can be suboptimal or return reached=false. The code comment labels the chain PROVABLY-OPTIMAL. With nothing dropped the extraction is exact.

extraction.research_question: Which self-rated Big Five traits predict friendship selection among just-acquainted late adolescents, separating selecting friends (ego), being selected as a friend (alter) and selecting similar friends (similarity), while controlling for network structure and sex; and how do friendship networks develop during acquaintanceship (pp. 513-514)?
extraction.theory: Main-effect accounts: extraversion as reward-seeking with more positive affect in social situations (Elphick et al. 1998; Fleeson et al. 2002; pp. 509-510); agreeableness as prosocial and altruistic behavior that makes people attractive friends (pp. 510, 528-529). Similarity-attraction (Byrne 1971) with reinforcement-affect (Clore and Byrne 1974) and uncertainty reduction (Berger and Calabrese 1975) mechanisms (pp. 511-512). Trait-specific similarity argued for extraversion (predictable interaction styles) and agreeableness (evolutionary game theory of altruism; Maynard Smith 1984; Gilchrist 2007) (pp. 512-513). Network closure: friendships form through existing ties, so transitivity and geodesic distance-2 are modeled (p. 514; definitions p. 519).
extraction.data: Sample: 205 psychology freshmen (M age 18.9, SD 1.6; 168 women = 82%; 189 Dutch = 92%) at Utrecht University, the Netherlands, nested in 10 introduction groups (of 20 groups of 16-24 students; 489 students randomly assigned; 378 agreed from 18 groups; 10 groups with more than 80% registration retained; 221 of 238 agreed, 93%; 205 of 221 retained at Wave 5, 93%) (pp. 514-516). Unit: directed friendship nominations among group members (dichotomized, 1 if 4 or higher on a 6-point scale), 5 monthly waves starting in week 2 of the first semester, i.e., roughly the first 4 months of university (pp. 515-516). Abstract says first year; the text covers about 4 months. Data-collection year not stated in text. Personality from single-item TIPI-r self-ratings on 1-7 bipolar scales, monthly (p. 516).
extraction.method: Stochastic actor-oriented models for network evolution estimated in SIENA (Snijders 2001; Snijders et al. 2006), run separately for each of 10 groups, then combined by multilevel meta-analysis of parameter estimates (Snijders and Baerveldt 2003) with group-size weighting (pp. 517-521). Network effects: outdegree, reciprocity, transitivity and geodesic distance-2 (GD-2). Covariates: sex and five Big Five traits, each with ego, alter and similarity parameters (18 parameters entered together; p. 520). Two-sided significance at p less than .01. Score tests (chi-square above 3.84, df 1) assessed whether transitivity and GD-2 improve fit (p. 520). Tested whether the variance of each mean effect differs from zero for between-group heterogeneity (p. 521).
extraction.identification: The text does not claim causal identification. Identification rests on longitudinal actor-based modeling of tie changes conditional on network state, simultaneous ego, alter and similarity parameters, controls for network effects and sex, and random assignment of students to introduction groups, which the authors say makes group-level confounding less likely (pp. 518, 531-532). The authors also note ego and alter effects may be confounded, so they estimate them jointly (p. 527).
extraction.scope: One Dutch university, psychology freshmen in one cohort, predominantly female and highly educated, observed over about the first 4 months of university (p. 531). Generalization to other demographics is explicitly not established (p. 531).

key_findings.finding: Networks became more cohesive over the first 3 months, then stabilized: average degree rose from 1.71 (Wave 1) to 2.64, 3.56, 3.67 and 3.64 (Wave 5); reciprocity .13 to .32; transitivity .33 to .45.

key_findings.finding: Friendship ties formed at Wave 2 persisted: 92% at Wave 3, 88% at Wave 4, 82% at Wave 5.
Extraversion ego effect was the only significant predictor of nominating more friends (more extraverted students nominated more friends).
key_findings.numbers: Extraversion ego .10 (SE .01), p less than .001

key_findings.finding: Agreeableness alter effect: higher agreeableness predicted being nominated as a friend; no other alter effect was significant.
key_findings.numbers: Agreeableness alter .14 (SE .01), p less than .001; Extraversion alter .01 (n.s.)

key_findings.finding: Similarity effects: individuals selected friends similar in Openness, Extraversion and Agreeableness, the strongest effects in the model.
key_findings.numbers: Openness 1.45 (SE .19); Extraversion 1.46 (SE .10); Agreeableness 1.55 (SE .03); all p less than .001

key_findings.finding: Similarity effects varied across groups for Openness, Extraversion and Agreeableness, but were significant in most groups: 7/10 (Openness), 8/10 (Extraversion), 10/10 (Agreeableness).
key_findings.numbers: variance .31 (p less than .001), .35 (p less than .001), .82 (p less than .01)

key_findings.finding: Sex: women nominated more friends (ego), and students selected same-sex friends (similarity).
key_findings.numbers: sex ego .29 (p less than .01); sex similarity .40 (p less than .001)

key_findings.numbers: Openness ego .02 (n.s.); Conscientiousness ego .02 (n.s.); Neuroticism ego .07 (n.s.); Neuroticism similarity .15 (n.s.); Conscientiousness similarity .17 (n.s.)

key_findings.numbers: repeated-measures ANOVAs F ranged .77 to 1.20, p greater than .10

key_findings.finding: Trait-specific similarity effects were larger than main effects, so matching on specific traits mattered more than absolute trait levels. Overall profile similarity was not modeled in this paper.
key_findings.numbers: similarity estimates (about 1.45 to 1.55) exceed ego and alter estimates (.01 to .14) in Table 2

limitations: Sample is highly educated and mostly female (82%) and Dutch (92%); forced same-gender and same-education choices may limit choice; authors note social homogamy may make the setting realistic (p. 531).
Only 10 introduction groups selected by participation rate (more than 80% registration); personality data unavailable for nonparticipants, so group selection bias cannot be adjusted (p. 531).

Nonparticipating group members rated themselves less neurotic (3.21 vs 3.62) and substantially less conscientious (3.92 vs 4.75); conscientiousness predicted attrition but not selection (pp. 516-517, 531).
With 10 groups, between-group variance estimates are imprecise (pp. 531-532).
Ties were dichotomized (friend or better vs not) because SIENA handles binary ties; a different cutoff could change results, though an alternative cutoff gave similar patterns (p. 532).
Only about 4 months of data; no network information after Month 4, so later development is unknown (pp. 527-528).
SIENA assumes ties are enduring states; the authors could only partly test this assumption over a short period (p. 518).
Measures are single-item TIPI-r self-ratings, not full Big Five scales (p. 516).
The abstract says first year of university, but the analyzed waves cover about 4 months.

summary_md:
Selfhout and colleagues followed 205 Dutch psychology freshmen in 10 randomly assigned introduction groups. They collected five monthly waves of friendship nominations, covering about the first 4 months of university, and analysed them with SIENA actor-oriented models. Each group was modelled separately and the results were then pooled by meta-analysis. Over the first three months the networks grew denser and then levelled off: average degree went from 1.71 to 3.64, and transitivity from .33 to .45. The structural terms were large in every group. Reciprocity was 1.73, and the score tests for transitivity and distance-2 ran from 15.7 to 93.4. A model that looks only at pairs would therefore misfit. Traits had small effects on individuals. Extraverts nominated more friends (ego effect .10), agreeable students were nominated more often (alter effect .14), and openness, conscientiousness and neuroticism had no ego or alter effect. Similarity in openness, extraversion and agreeableness had the largest effects (1.45 to 1.55), but they varied across groups: they were significant in 7, 8 and 10 of the 10 groups respectively.

The paper does not touch lobbying, legislators or elections. Its value for Paul's systems is narrow and comes in two parts. First, it shows that personality matters mostly for pairs of people, through how similar they are. A trait level on one person matters much less. Second, it shows how to test similarity: inside a model that also controls for reciprocity and closure, because a raw correlation can mislead. That bears on the persona-homophily null and on the receptivity layer, where every input describes one member. It also bears on the cosponsor forecaster, which has no reciprocity or closure features, and on the stance co-movement test, which is only a pair-level test. Transfer is weak throughout. These are self-rated single-item traits among strangers forming friendships. Legislators meeting lobbyists, or building cosponsorship records over years, are a different setting.

bearings.paper_claim: Trait similarity is the strongest selection effect: openness 1.45, extraversion 1.46, agreeableness 1.55 (all p<.001), against ego and alter effects of .01 to .14. It is estimated jointly with outdegree, reciprocity, transitivity, distance-2 and sex, and it varies by group: significant in 7/10, 8/10 and 10/10 groups. Overall profile similarity was not modelled here; the authors' 2009 paper on the same sample found it did not predict friendship intensity.
bearings.system_side: The persona-homophily gate correlates persona compatibility (sum of agency and communion differences, IPC complementarity, communion match only, both warm) with static cosponsor tie weights, with the party confound removed. All four models gave |r| <= 0.015, so the homophily edge weighting stays off.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfer is weak. The paper's similarity effect appears while self-rated strangers choose friends in the first months, with network structure held fixed. Cosponsorship among sitting legislators is an established, party- and committee-driven tie, not a choice among strangers. The paper does not overturn the null and is no reason to re-propose homophily edge weighting. Its one transferable point: a cross-sectional correlation with no reciprocity or closure controls, using a combined two-trait distance, is a different test from trait-specific similarity estimated inside a selection model. The null therefore holds for the test that was run, not for homophily in general. Any SIENA rerun would be new analysis and would stay UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-psychometrics#Agency-communion persona channel|Agency-communion persona channel]]

bearings.paper_claim: Effects of one person's own traits are small next to similarity effects. Extraversion predicts making more ties (ego .10), agreeableness predicts being chosen (alter .14), and openness has no ego or alter effect (.02, n.s.).
bearings.system_side: seed_prob uses only the member's own traits. The default behavioural basis is 0.60 + .10 cooperation_v2 + .06 breadth + .04 visibility; the non-default lexical basis is 0.60 + .10A + .06O + .04E, on the reasoning that agreeable, open and extraverted members take meetings. Nothing describes the match between a lobbyist or recruiter and the member.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfer is weak. The paper measures friendship nomination, not whether a contacted official acts. Within that limit, it gives no support to the openness term in the lexical basis. The agreeableness result concerns being approached, not acting once approached. The paper's main point, that pairwise similarity outweighs individual levels, shows a dyadic term is missing, but there is no legislative evidence for adding one, and the system's own persona-homophily test came out null.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)|Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)]]

bearings.paper_claim: Reciprocity 1.73 (SE .11), transitivity .14 (SE .02) and distance-2 -.52 (SE .06) were all significant. Adding transitivity and distance-2 improved fit in all 10 groups (chi-square 15.68 to 93.43, df 1), so a model of independent pairs misfits network tie formation.
bearings.paper_location: Table 2 p. 524; p. 524
bearings.system_side: The ridge-logistic forecaster uses pair and individual features: prior sponsor affinity, prior member cosponsorships, network degree and eigenvector, NOMINATE distances, same party/state/chamber, committee features. It has no term for reciprocation (has the sponsor previously cosponsored this member's bills?) and none for closure (shared cosponsor partners).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfer is moderate in method and weak in evidence. Reciprocity and closure in friendship nominations do not establish the same effects in cosponsorship; the component's own question about Brandenberger reciprocity is the legislative test. Here 'reciprocity' means tie reciprocation and must not be confused with the money reciprocity that is still unvalidated (D-104..D-108). Any added feature counts only after the frozen 265,396-prediction forecast is scored against a non-circular outcome, and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

bearings.paper_claim: Stochastic actor-oriented models estimate tie selection conditional on the current network state, with ego, alter and similarity terms for each covariate, and pool groups by multilevel meta-analysis. The cited extensions (Steglich et al. 2006; Burk et al. 2007) model networks and behaviour together, which separates selection from influence.
bearings.paper_location: Method pp. 517-521; references Steglich 2006, Burk 2007
bearings.system_side: Neighbour co-movement counts members who move in the same versus the opposite direction as their cosponsor or HCoI neighbours, quarter to quarter. The result was null on both layers. Neighbour imputation proposals are built on this (77% sign agreement under masking).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfer is moderate in method only. The paper itself models selection and not influence, so it gives no evidence on stance contagion. A joint network-and-behaviour SIENA model is the standard way to ask whether ties drive stance change or stance similarity drives ties. That would need panel waves of cosponsor ties and quarterly stances. It would be new analysis, UNVERIFIED until reproduced, and its pooled estimates must be reported by stratum (party, chamber) or marked UNSTRATIFIED.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation|Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation]]

gaps_exposed: No component has a pairwise similarity or compatibility term between the source (a lobbyist, or a recruiting member) and the target. Receptivity, seed_prob and edge_mult are all single-member multipliers, although the paper finds similarity effects about 10 times larger than individual effects. The system's own persona-homophily test is null, so this is a recorded gap, not a recommendation.

The cosponsor forecaster has no reciprocation feature (did the sponsor previously cosponsor this member?) and no closure feature (shared cosponsor partners). The paper shows such structural terms improved fit in every group it studied.

The homophily and co-movement tests are cross-sectional or pair-level and are not conditioned on network structure. No model jointly estimates selection and influence, so the cosponsor-stance null cannot separate 'no influence' from 'selection hides it'.
flags: The paper's 'reciprocity' is the reciprocation of friendship nominations. It must not be read as support for the money reciprocity in the competitiveness multiplier, which remains NOT validated (D-104..D-108).

The pooled similarity estimates come from 10 groups with significant between-group variance (openness .31, extraversion .35, agreeableness .82). Quote them with strata (significant in 7/10, 8/10 and 10/10 groups) or mark them UNSTRATIFIED.

No conflict with the two rejected SNA proposals. The paper dichotomises ties at 'friend or better' because SIENA requires binary ties. That is a method constraint, not an argument for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalisation, and it must not be cited as one.
The paper gives no basis for re-proposing persona-homophily edge weighting. The system's gate (|r| <= 0.015) stands. Any SIENA-style rerun is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

Window and denominator: 205 students in 10 groups (out of 20 introduction groups), 5 monthly waves over about 4 months, single-item TIPI-r self-ratings, 82% women. The abstract's 'first year' overstates the window.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It is nearest to his position on the receptivity layer, that psychological traits should enter as edge parameters (Oropeza), and to his agency/communion node design. The paper broadly agrees that personality acts on ties, and mainly through pairwise similarity, not through one person's trait level. That is closer to Paul's edge framing than to the system's single-member seed_prob. His notes are stale in one respect: they do not record that the system tested persona homophily against cosponsor ties and found nothing (all |r| <= 0.015), so the edge idea is unearned for now. This paper does not change that verdict, because friendship among strangers is a weak proxy for legislative ties.

related.why: Supplies the agency/communion persona measurement that the system used in its homophily test. Selfhout supplies the selection-model evidence that trait similarity, not trait level, drives tie formation.
Palm reviews personality as a moderator of persuasion, the monadic receptivity question. Selfhout shows that in tie formation the pairwise similarity effect outweighs individual levels.
Haythornthwaite gives the directed, tie-strength SNA framing Paul values. Selfhout gives a longitudinal directed-tie model in which reciprocity and transitivity are estimated, not assumed.

backlinks.why: Offline Big Five friendship-network selection study. It is a stronger, longitudinal test of the trait homophily that Celli only describes.

extraction.document_type: Research article: analytical (heterogeneous mean-field) plus numerical simulation (gradient ascent, stochastic hill-climbing) on a single empirical network. No empirical election or lobbying data.
